rooms/keys/backfill/0.2.note: No host. Nothing maps a room to its host — rooms are portable — so the caller names the one to fetch from; a recipient guessing one would contact a party of its own choosing with its principal's credentials.

rooms/keys/chain/0.2.note: Neither rungs nor a floor. A delivery with nothing in it extends nothing and forgets nothing; it is refused rather than answered.
An empty `links` array. Absent is how a request that only relays a floor is spelled; an empty array is a second spelling of the same thing.
A rung claiming epoch 1. The room's first epoch has no predecessor, so a rung numbered 1 wraps something that is not an earlier epoch's key.

rooms/keys/file-key/0.2.note: No purpose. Sealing and opening derive under different epochs — the current one, or the one the file was sealed under — and a custodian that guessed would hand a sealing caller a key members cannot use, or an opening caller a key that does not open the file.
A file identifier that is not 32 bytes. The identifier is the derivation's salt and the guarantee that no two files share a key; a short or guessable one weakens both.
A purpose outside the two. `export` or `rotate` would be a different power — releasing a room-wide key — which this task deliberately cannot express.
Asking for the room's storage key by name. The storage key never leaves the custodian; only a key derived for one file does.
A response carrying more than one file's key. Each release covers one file, so that a key leaked from the caller exposes that file and nothing else.

rooms/keys/key-package/0.2.note: No invitation. 0.2 requires one: it is what authorizes the mint, names the member, and identifies the outstanding KeyPackage a second surface is given.

Asking for a fresh KeyPackage. A second mint while one is outstanding is what leaves an acceptance begun in one surface unfinishable from another; the recipient decides, from the room, member and invitation, whether to return the one it holds.
Bare/unnamespaced ext key — SPEC §4.5.1 requires every immediate child of ext to be reverse-DNS namespaced.
No `alreadyMinted`. A surface finishing an acceptance needs to know whether the KeyPackage is the one another surface may already have sent.
No `expiresAt`. 0.2 requires it: it bounds how long an acceptance begun elsewhere can be finished with this KeyPackage.

rooms/keys/label/0.1.note: No change at all. A request naming a room and a member and nothing to set or remove asks for nothing; `minProperties` is what refuses it, since `required` alone would accept it.
No member. The label is keyed by room AND member — a person holding one room as two personas keeps one for each — so the key holder never infers whose label is meant.
A member that is not a DID.
A detail both given and removed. dependentSchemas makes the two mutually exclusive, so a request cannot be read two ways.
removeDescription: false. Only `true` is meaningful; `false` would be a second spelling of "unchanged".
label: null. Removal is `removeLabel`, never a null, so libraries that map absent and null to one option cannot confuse "unchanged" with "remove".
An empty label. Removal is `removeLabel`; an empty string would be a third spelling of it.
A line break in the label. A name is one line; a surface listing rooms must not be made to render a second.
An escape character in the notes. Line breaks and tabs are allowed there; other control characters are not, since a terminal surface would interpret them.
An empty tag list. Removing every tag is `removeTags`; there is one way to say "none".
A repeated tag. Tags are a set.
A request to share the label. There is no such member: the label is never sent to the room, its host or a community, so no request carries a destination for it.
Bare/unnamespaced ext key — SPEC §4.5.1 requires every immediate child of ext to be reverse-DNS namespaced.
An empty personal label. A key holder holding no detail holds no label and omits `personal`; an object carrying only `updatedAt` would be a second way to say so.
No `changed`. A caller retrying a request needs to know whether this one wrote anything.

A subject. A recipient answers for its own principal and for nobody else; a member naming whose rooms to list is the shape of a task this one is not.
Paging members. Rooms are bounded by how many a person is in, so there is no cursor to issue and none to accept — a caller that sent one would be relying on behaviour no recipient implements.
Bare/unnamespaced ext key — SPEC §4.5.1 requires every immediate child of ext to be reverse-DNS namespaced.

rooms/keys/list/0.2.note: A roomId filter. rooms/keys/profile/read/0.1.note: No host. Nothing maps a room to its host, so the caller must name it.
A host that is not a DID. The recipient resolves the host as a DID and speaks only the transports its document advertises; a URL would be an address the caller chose.
A record key. The caller cannot know where the profile is — that is the point — so it cannot name one.
Bare/unnamespaced ext key — SPEC §4.5.1 requires every immediate child of ext to be reverse-DNS namespaced.

An icon URL. A profile carries nothing a reader fetches: a fetched icon would tell whoever serves it which member opened which room.
A record key. The recipient computes where the profile goes; a caller choosing it could put the room's name at a key the host can read.
Bare/unnamespaced ext key — SPEC §4.5.1 requires every immediate child of ext to be reverse-DNS namespaced.
An outcome the specification does not define.

rooms/keys/seal/0.2.note: No version. The version is bound into the ciphertext, so a request without one is asking for a record that cannot be bound to where it will live — and there is no defaulting that would be honest, because only the caller knows which write shape it is about to use.
A negative version. Versions are assigned from a monotonic counter that starts at 1, and `0` is the create-only precondition — nothing below that names a record that can exist.
No plaintext. Sealing nothing is not a coherent request; the member is the whole input.

The record's parts sent separately. Splitting title/body/tags would let a host read the shape of the material from ciphertext lengths — the sealed tiers seal one blob for exactly this reason, so the structure belongs inside `plaintext`, not beside it.
Bare/unnamespaced ext key — SPEC §4.5.1 requires every immediate child of ext to be reverse-DNS namespaced.
`signAsPrincipal` as a string — a flag that asks the key holder to sign as the member must be unambiguous, never a truthy string a parser might read either way.
The unsigned body sent as an object beside `plaintext` — the body is sealed whole from `plaintext`, and a second copy beside it is material that would not be sealed.
Standard base64 with padding in `plaintext` — the body is unpadded base64url.
Response without `sealed` — the writer would have nothing to store.

rooms/owner/group/add/0.3.note: No member. An owner admits a party, not a KeyPackage: naming who is meant is what lets the recipient refuse a KeyPackage for somebody else.

A KeyPackage in standard base64 with padding. The family carries MLS messages as base64url without padding, and accepting both would give one KeyPackage two spellings.

Bare/unnamespaced ext key — SPEC §4.5.1 requires every immediate child of ext to be reverse-DNS namespaced.

rooms/owner/group/create/0.1.note: No signingKeyId. Control of the room's key is the entitlement to found its group; a request that omits it asks the recipient to decide whose room this is.
A member that is not a DID. The leaf identifies a party other members' key holders will see in every commit; a bare name identifies nobody.
A group secret offered by the caller. The group's secrets are created inside the recipient; a request that carried one would let the caller choose the key schedule every member then trusts.
Bare/unnamespaced ext key — SPEC §4.5.1 requires every immediate child of ext to be reverse-DNS namespaced.

rooms/owner/group/remove/0.4.note: No member. Removal names whom it removes; a recipient asked to choose would be deciding who leaves.
No host. Removal is an epoch advance at the room's host; without one there is nowhere to advance, and a local-only removal would seal to keys no other member holds.
A member that is not a DID. A leaf identifies a party by DID; a name identifies nobody the group knows.
An unbounded reason. Free text carried to another party is bounded (SPEC §7.3 item 19).
Bare/unnamespaced ext key — SPEC §4.5.1 requires every immediate child of ext to be reverse-DNS namespaced.
A mirror that is not a DID. A host is addressed by its DID; a URL here would be a location the recipient is induced to call.

A response that does not say whether the member was withdrawn. Since 0.4 a private room's removal withdraws nothing, and a response a surface could read either way would let it report a withdrawal that never happened.
A response with no epoch. Every removal, on either tier, advances the room, and the epoch is what the removed member holds no key for.

rooms/owner/group/renew/0.2.note: No host. Renewal is an epoch advance at the room's host; a group advanced without one would seal to keys the host refuses, and every write after it would fail.
No room. A recipient asked to choose which room to renew would be deciding which room's epoch moves.
A host that is not a DID. The epoch advance is addressed to the host's DID, and the request's proof covers that recipient; a URL names no party a proof can be bound to.

A member to renew for. Renewal changes no membership; a member named here would be a removal or an admission wearing another task's name, and those are rooms/owner/group/remove and rooms/owner/group/add.
An unbounded reason. Free text carried to another party is bounded (SPEC §7.3 item 19).
Bare/unnamespaced ext key — SPEC §4.5.1 requires every immediate child of ext to be reverse-DNS namespaced.
A response at epoch 1. Renewal advances the epoch, and a room is registered at 1, so the epoch after any renewal is at least 2.

rooms/owner/invite/0.1.note: No signingKeyId. The recipient signs AS the room, and which key does that is the entire authorization story — a request that omits it is asking the recipient to choose, which is the one decision it must never make on the caller's behalf.
No subject. Every credential here names who it is for; one without a subject confers on nobody, and a schema that allowed it would let a producer mint a credential it could not explain.
Bare/unnamespaced ext key — SPEC §4.5.1 requires every immediate child of ext to be reverse-DNS namespaced.

An unknown member — additionalProperties: false catches `reason`. Whatever is placed beside the credential travels with it to the invitee, so a free-form note here is a note the room's host may end up reading.
validUntil as a date rather than a date-time. An invitation's window is the whole of its safety, and a value that cannot be ordered against an issuedAt is not a window.

An empty actions list. It confers nothing rather than everything — but those are exactly the two readings a careless consumer might choose between, so the input is refused rather than the choice left open.
No actions at all. Same reasoning as the empty list, and the more likely typo.

An action outside the enum. `delete` is not a room verb — retraction is a curation judgement (`curate`) and purging is a host operation, so a grant naming it would confer something no host implements.

A role instead of a party. Membership is an explicit set of parties, never a role — a room that admitted a role would be a room whose membership its host could compute, and the host is the party the design keeps membership away from.

No signing key. The recipient signs as the room with a key named explicitly; one looked up from the room would be a mapping nothing maintains.
A caller-chosen revokedAt. The recipient stamps the time it signs; a caller who dated a withdrawal could reach back past a re-admission, or forward past grants not yet made.

The same host twice. Each host is delivered to once and reported once.

A prune marker that removed nothing. A prune that removed no record leaves no mark — `removed` is at least 1 — because a marker a reader must rebuild on is not something to send for nothing.

No kinds. A prune says what it removes; an empty request that removed whatever the host thought eligible would be a destructive act nobody specified.

A kind outside the two. `expired` is the plausible wrong guess: a record's `validUntil` is sealed, and a host cannot see it, so expiry is never a host's to prune by — a curator retracts expired records and the tombstones age out.

Naming the records to remove. A prune removes what the room's stated retention makes eligible, which every member could read in advance; removing records an administrator picks by key is a different act, and not one this task performs.

An override of the retention carried in the request. Eligibility is decided by the retention in force, which members can read; a prune carrying its own would remove records under a rule nobody was shown. Change the retention first, with rooms/records/retention/set.
`dryRun: false` on a real prune. Absent is how a real prune is spelled; two spellings of one meaning are two things for readers to disagree about.

0.1's `prune.at` does not exist in 0.2; it is `prunedAt` (rooms/_shared/0.2).

vtc/vetting/vetters/grant/0.1.note: `memberDid` is required — a grant names the member it makes a vetter.
`memberDid` is a DID, not a display name or member handle. The role credential's subject is the DID the vetter signs statements with.
A role credential valid for less than a day cannot outlast the vetting it is meant to cover; 86400 seconds is the floor.
Two years (63072000 seconds) is the ceiling. Eligibility is re-granted, not granted for good.

`cursor` is a non-empty token. An empty string is not the first page — omit the member instead.
`language` is a BCP 47 tag, not a language name.
`country` is an upper-case ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code, the same form a profile stores.
`method` comes from the shared VettingMethod vocabulary. `phone` is not a vetting method.

vtc/vetting/vetters/profile/0.1.note: `listed` is required. The profile replaces the whole stored profile, so a missing flag would have to be guessed — and guessing `true` publishes a vetter who never said so.
`methods` is required, even when unlisting. A partial payload is not a patch: the profile is replaced as a whole.
A vetter offers at least one method; an empty list could never match a request.
Methods come from the shared VettingMethod vocabulary, lowerCamelCase. `in-person` is not one.
A method is listed once; `uniqueItems` refuses a repeat.
`displayName` is 1–128 characters when present. An empty string is not an absent name — omit the member instead.
Language tags are BCP 47, not language names.
`location.country` is an upper-case ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code. `de` is lower case.
`location` needs a country; a city on its own is ambiguous.
A location is coarse — country, region, city. There is no street address member, and a vetter's home is not something a listing should carry.
Documentation classes use the shared lowerCamelCase token. `national-id` is not one.
An event date is `YYYY-MM-DD`. A date-time is refused: events are listed by UTC date.
An event carries `endDate`; a single-day event repeats its `startDate`.
An event `url` is https. A plain-http link would let anyone on the applicant's network rewrite where they go.
No `vetterDid` member. The vetter is the authenticated sender; a payload naming a DID would invite a profile for someone else.
